newsitem.title: USA: Fed believes NAIRU above 5.5 pct, economists say.
newsitem.headline: Fed believes NAIRU above 5.5 pct, economists say.

text.p: A string of tightening biases coinciding with a low jobless rate indicates the Federal Reserve regards a 5.5-percent unemployment rate as potentially inflationary, economists said on Friday.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) introduced a tightening bias in July 1996 as the unemployment rate for the March-to-May period -- the latest data available at the time -- averaged 5.5 percent. The jobless rate has hovered below 5.5 percent since then and the tightening bias has remained in place.

"I'm sure most people in the whole Federal Reserve System -- including at the FOMC -- and people elsewhere subscribe to one version or another of the NAIRU theory," said former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder.
"Many people would think an unemployment rate lower than 5.5 percent is below the NAIRU (non-accelerating inflation rate of unemployment)," Blinder said.

"We managed to stay there without an inkling of inflation acceleration, and the longer that situation persists, the more believable it becomes the NAIRU is actually lower than 5.5 percent," Blinder pointed out.
Blinder, who now holds the chair of economics at Princeton University, said the Fed is engaged in an experiment to see if the NAIRU, often described as 5-3/4 percent, has edged lower.

"Whether it is accidentally or purposefully, and I think it was largely accidentally, we are running an experiment to see whether an unemployment rate below 5.5 percent will or will not cause an acceleration in inflation," Blinder said.

The Fed has a bias in place without acting upon it for an unprecedented seven months. The FOMC, in its December minutes, explained the bias was an indication of the direction of the next policy rather than a signal of an imminent move.
"The jury is out on the (NAIRU) question. And that is one reason for the asymmetric directive," Blinder explained.
Though central bankers are seldom inclined to experiment, Blinder stressed the risks are limited and the protracted bias underscores the Fed's vigilance.
"Even if we are below NAIRU, it's going to take a very long time to actually see the difference in inflation because you don't see it until the momentum builds," Blinder stressed.
By Blinder's own estimate, it would take a jobless rate at a full percentage point below NAIRU over a period of one year to result in a half-percentage point rise in inflation.

"Suppose we were 1/4 percent below NAIRU for a year, this would be 1/8 percent added to inflation, and you can't pick that up in data because the measurement is not that tight," the Princeton professor concluded.
Goldman, Sachs and Co chief economist William Dudley stated "it would be very hard for the Fed to think NAIRU is not above 5.5 percent, given the employment data and Employment Cost Index."
Dudley noted wages started to rise faster as the jobless rate fell to 5.5 percent, which also coincided with the introduction of a tightening bias.
"The bulk of the evidence suggests NAIRU is above 5.5 percent and that is what most people at the Fed believe," Dudley said. "They did not know before. Now, they do know."
Dudley also stressed the December FOMC minutes explained the Fed could "afford to wait for the time being, which implies they'll have to tighten, though they don't know exactly when."

Chief economist Stuart Hoffman at PNC Bank Corp concurs that "one can infer the Fed feels on guard when the unemployment rate is below 5.5 percent." He cautioned the notion of NAIRU is open for debate and not a sure guide for monetary policy.

"Even if you think the theory is applicable, one has to be more vigilant in trying to pinpoint where NAIRU is. It's the reason for people on the FOMC to be a little more patient in acting on the premise the number is about 5.5 percent."

Hoffman said the extended stretch of tightening bias amounted to a compromise at the FOMC between those who strictly adhere to the NAIRU notion and wanted a prompt tightening, and those prepared to wait and see whether full employment can coexist with limited inflation pressure.

"We know there were some people who probably wanted to move last fall," Hoffman pointed out. "Within the Fed, the bias is a compromise, a way to garner a consensus and be poised to raise rates if the evidence becomes persuasive. It keeps everybody semi-happy."
Hoffman also described the lengthy bias string as "a way to alert markets the Fed is on heightened surveillance. In that sense, it serves a useful purpose."

Hoffman further pointed out the Fed, in the December FOMC minutes, stated its intention "to act promptly" if inflation were to rise or as "higher inflation expectations become embedded in financial markets and economic decision making" -- the markets' own take on the NAIRU paradigm.
